title: Claude for Long-Horizon Tasks — Lance Martin, Anthropic

primary.label: Agent Architecture & Harnesses
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 100%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central subject is agent harness architecture—decoupling brain from hands, build-verify loops, org-level multiplayer harnesses, and the control plane around models for long-horizon tasks. Content spans general-purpose agent harness patterns and developer-facing surfaces like Managed Agents, Agent SDK, and Claude Tag. The talk covers designing harness architecture, building with verification loops, and operating org-level proactive agents in production. Assumes familiarity with Claude API surfaces, agent harness concepts, and context engineering for long-horizon tasks. Technical conference presentation with live demonstrations and audience Q&A. All cited evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript with direct excerpts from the talk.

summary: Lance Martin frames Claude as a light source and products as windows, noting that as model task horizons grow, the appropriate product surface shifts. Opus 3-era models did 10–20 minutes; Claude Code-era did ~1 hour; now longer horizons unlock async agents. API surfaces evolved: Messages API, Agent SDK, and Managed Agents. Theme one—decoupling brain from hands—makes the harness stateless, talking to an append-only session log that reaches out to sandbox containers, with credentials in a separate vault, improving reliability, security, and context persistence. Theme two—use verifiers—separates verification into an independent context window to avoid confabulation, enabling build-verify loops demonstrated via a parameter golf benchmark. Theme three—self-learning—uses in-band memory writing. Continual Learning Bench shows newer models write more strategic, generalizable abstractions to memory. A 'dreaming' offline process corrects memory errors, demonstrated in Pokémon where an incorrect memory caused Claude to fall through a trapdoor in 5/5 replicates, but dreaming fixed it. Anthropic has run many evaluations confirming dreaming improves performance for intuitive reasons, though users should run their own evals to confirm it's worth the offline compute. Theme four—org-level harnesses—highlights Claude Tag as a multiplayer harness with its own identity and organizational context, enabling proactive async agents that alert users, deduplicate findings, and provide day-one access. Q&A addresses why frontier models lead on long-horizon tasks (memory, security, and architecture must converge), and memory substrate choice: use general programmable substrates rather than prescriptive schemas, following the bitter lesson that models manage their own memory better than hand-designed schemas.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Claude's task horizon grew from 10–20 minutes to ~1 hour to today's longer horizons enabling true async agents.
Decoupling the brain (stateless harness) from hands (sandbox containers) via an append-only session log improves reliability, security, and context persistence.
Verification should use an independent context window tuned for critical verification, not the same context that did the work.
In-band memory writing improves across model generations: higher-capacity models write generalizable abstractions, not just specific facts.
Offline 'dreaming' corrects memory errors; evaluations confirm it improves performance, though users should run their own evals to justify the offline compute cost.
Org-level harnesses like Claude Tag provide multiplayer, proactive async agents with shared identity, organizational context, and day-one access.
Memory substrates should be general and programmable; prescribing memory schemas degrades performance because models manage their own memory better.
Frontier models lead on long-horizon tasks because memory, security, and architecture must converge—not model capability alone.
Build-verify loops paired with high-capacity models are a powerful primitive for long-running async work.
Understand how Claude's task horizon has evolved and which product surfaces suit each capability level

sections.title: Introduction and Task Horizon Evolution
sections.summary: Lance Martin introduces Anthropic's view on async agents, using the metaphor of Claude as a light source and products as windows. He traces task horizon growth: Opus 3-era models did 10–20 minutes, Claude Code-era did ~1 hour, and now longer horizons unlock async. API surfaces evolved: Messages API, Agent SDK, and Managed Agents (released April).

sections.title: Theme 1: Decoupling Brain from Hands
sections.summary: Explains separating the harness (brain) from execution containers (hands). Initial approach placed both in one container, risking session loss and credential exposure. The new architecture makes the harness stateless, talking to an append-only session log that reaches out to sandbox containers. Credentials stay in a separate vault. This also benefits context engineering—context is persistent, non-destructive, and append-only.

sections.title: Theme 2: Use Verifiers
sections.summary: Addresses self-grading in the same context causing confabulation. Solution: separate verification into an independent context window tuned for critical verification. Build-verify loops run until an independent verifier confirms desired outcomes. Demonstrated via parameter golf benchmark where Opus 4.7 and a frontier mythos-class model iterated to completion.

sections.title: Theme 3: Self-Learning and Memory Systems
sections.summary: Draws analogy to human memory: hippocampus writes short-term traces; dreams consolidate to cortex. Claude uses in-band memory tools. Claude plays Pokémon shows Sonnet 3.5 wrote low-quality memories with limited progress, while newer models write strategic notes and progress further, demonstrating improvement in self-learning across generations.

sections.title: Continual Learning Bench and Dreaming
sections.summary: Continual Learning Bench (sequential SQL QA with in-band memory) shows performance improves across model generations. Higher-capacity models write generalizable abstractions rather than specific facts. Introduces 'dreaming'—an offline process to consolidate and correct memory errors. Pokémon example: an incorrect memory caused Claude to fall through a trapdoor in 5/5 replicates; dreaming corrected the error. Memory traces show no-memory baseline stuck, memory backtracking through trapdoor, dreaming fixing errors and progressing.

sections.title: Theme 4: Org-Level Harnesses and Q&A
sections.summary: Introduces org-level harnesses like Claude Tag, a multiplayer harness with its own identity and organizational context, contrasting with single-player agents. Benefits include deduplication, internal research, day-one access, and proactive alerting. Q&A covers why frontier models lead on long-horizon tasks (memory, security, architecture must converge) and memory substrate choice: use general programmable substrates rather than prescriptive schemas, following the bitter lesson that models manage their own memory better.

sections.title: Closing Q&A on Dreaming Evaluations
sections.summary: Final audience question asks how we know dreaming corrections are correct. Lance notes evaluations are the way to confirm this, citing the Pokémon anecdote as an intuitive illustration and mentioning Anthropic has run many evals showing dreaming improves performance. Users should run their own evals in their own context to confirm dreaming is worth the offline compute cost. Talk concludes.

demonstrations: Parameter golf benchmark (OpenAI): trained a small model on 8x100 GPUs in under 10 minutes using a verifier loop with Managed Agents and outcomes, testing Opus 4.7 and a frontier mythos-class model
Claude plays Pokémon: comparing in-band memory writing quality and game progress between Sonnet 3.5 and a newer model (4.6)
Continual Learning Bench: sequential SQL QA task where models write memory between steps, showing performance improves across model generations
Pokémon dreaming experiment: incorrect memory caused Claude to fall through a trapdoor in 5/5 replicates; offline dreaming corrected the error and enabled progress
limitations: Async agent experience is poor when models can only do ~1 hour of work—models hit errors over short periods
Self-grading within the same context window causes confabulation and odd behavior
Putting harness and sandbox in the same container risks losing the session if the container dies
Placing credentials in the same container as the agent poses security concerns as models become more capable
Sonnet 3.5's in-band memory writing was tactical and not strategic, limiting game progress
In-band memory writing can introduce incorrect or locally optimal memories that persist without an offline correction process
Prescriptive memory schemas degrade performance compared to letting models manage their own memory
Dreaming requires offline compute; users should run their own evaluations to confirm it's worth the cost
quantitativeClaims: Opus 3-era models (2024) could do 10–20 minutes of autonomous work
Claude Code-era models could do ~1 hour of work
Parameter golf benchmark required training with 8x100 GPUs in less than 10 minutes
Sonnet 3.5 wrote tactical, low-quality in-band memories with limited game progress
Newer model (4.6) wrote more strategic memories and achieved further game progress
Frontier mythos-class models reach 12+ hour regime on METR-style benchmarks
Pokémon trapdoor failure occurred in 5 out of 5 replicates with raw memory store; dreaming corrected the error
